card.does: Turns to an angle you choose, and holds it.
card.popularMechanics: The same part steers a radio-controlled car and moves a camera gimbal.
card.safetyNote: A real servo motor comes with small horns and screws, so build with an adult nearby.

failureModes.cardLine: No signal: the arm stays where it is and hums.
failureModes.hint: This servo motor is waiting for a signal
failureModes.teachingNote: A servo motor turns to the angle its signal asks for. With power but no signal it has nothing to follow, so it holds where it is and hums. A microcontroller gives that signal on a signal line (yellow), and no Level 2 part gives one.

failureModes.cardLine: No complete circuit: the arm stays still, with no hum.
failureModes.hint: This servo motor is not in a loop with the battery pack
failureModes.teachingNote: Without a complete loop from plus, through the servo motor and back to minus, it gets no power, so its arm stays still and it makes no sound.

failureModes.cardLine: Too little power: the arm turns slowly and weakly, or not at all.
failureModes.hint: This servo motor is not getting enough power
failureModes.teachingNote: A servo motor is made for 4.8 to 6 volts. On less, such as one 2-cell battery pack, its arm turns slowly and pushes weakly, and below about 2.5 volts it does nothing at all.

failureModes.cardLine: Wires swapped: the arm stays still, with no hum.
failureModes.hint: This servo motor's plus and minus are swapped
failureModes.teachingNote: A servo motor works only with plus to plus. Wired the other way round it does nothing at all, and a real one can be damaged this way.

failureModes.cardLine: Too much to push: the arm stops and hums.
failureModes.hint: This servo motor cannot move its load
failureModes.teachingNote: A servo motor can push or hold only so much. Asked for more, its arm stops short of its angle and hums while it draws the most current it ever draws, so the battery pack drains fast.
